DAYLIGHT BURNED OUT AND BLOWN OUT article by Jody Duncan After months of rugged live-action shooting in Slovakia for Dragonheart, director Rob Cohen returned to Los Angeles only to dive immediately into Daylight, a new action-suspense film released by Universal Pictures. The back-to-back production schedules were especially harrowing, since Cohen was overseeing postproduction for the former film - including the unprecedented creation, by Industrial Light & Magic, of a lead character that was entirely computer generated - while directing the latter in Rome. Realizing that the logistics of such double-duty filmmaking would be complicated by the long distance between the director - who would spend a total of seven months in Europe - and stateside effects teams at work on both movies, Cohen and executive producer Raffaella de Laurentiis nonetheless chose Cinecitta Studios, in Rome, with an eye toward filming Daylight in the grand old Hollywood style, on massively-scaled sets consuming many acres of backlot space. Daylight is a race-against-the-clock rescue story set within New York's underground transit system. When a traffic accident results in a toxic explosion of catastrophic proportions, both ends of a fictitious tunnel linking New Jersey and New York are sealed. Trapped beneath the Hudson River, and with water levels rising, the survivors of the blast come to rely on a former emergency medical services chief, Kit Latura (Sylvester Stallone), to find a way out of the collapsing tunnel and deliver them into daylight. Cinecitta's ample backlot easily accommodated the unusually large-scaled interiors and exteriors mandated by a film set almost entirely within a large underground thoroughfare. Production designer Benjamin Fernandez oversaw the construction of a nearly one-third-mile-long tunnel at the studio, as well as constructs representing tunnel Via a digital matte painting from Illusion Arts, a tunnel entrance built in Rome for the Rob Cohen film, Daylight, was surrounded by buildings and a river setting that placed it in New York. entrances, plazas and control rooms. Through numerous stages of storyboarding, Cohen - who wanted to realize as much of the film's action as possible practically and in-camera - determined which effects could be reasonably achieved on those full-scale sets. With veteran physical effects supervisor Kit West orchestrating, cars were rolled and crashed, structures were made to collapse, a million gallons of water were pumped through the set, and numerous explosions were ignited. Inevitably, however, some two hundred shots were relegated, from the beginning, to miniature, bluescreen and digital effects techniques. A twominute explosion sequence featuring an unusual, almost predatory fire, and the thrill-ride-like 'blowout'- which would transport characters through the top of the tunnel in a high-pressure geyser of water - accounted for a significant portion of the visual effects; and both sequences were given to Industrial Light & Magic. Throughout production, visual effects supervisor Scott Farrar divided his time between the ILM facility in San Rafael - where, with co-supervisor Joe Letteri, he directed the miniature and digital effects effort - and Cinecitta, where he oversaw the bluescreen photography for ILM's slate of fifty-some shots. Action sequences that could not be achieved practically were assigned to miniature and bluescreen photography units headed by miniature supervisor Grant McCune and director of miniature photography Bill Taylor. Both the ILM and production bluescreen units were housed on stages at Cinecitta, where - among other things - elements were photographed for those shots that were too dangerous to attempt on the set, such as a view of the toxic fire hitting a camper and knocking its shell off the truck bed. "The camper shell swings into a car behind it," Cohen explained, "breaking the windshield as the woman driver dives out of the way a split-second before impact." Farrar designed an effects approach that avoided the obvious danger of such a stunt. On the set, the camper shell CINEFEX 68 • 15 SUMMONSED

The initial ascent was shot on a twenty-foot-tall set at Cinecitta; but for up-angles revealing the character climbing higher into the shaft, a greenscreen was hung above the set to facilitate the compositing of miniature photography behind the actor. A twenty-foot-long miniature, laid horizontally for ease of access, was filmed by Taylor and McCune at Grant McCune Design in Van Nuys, as were all of the miniature sequences. "The modelmakers at Grant's shop carefully arranged dangling chains and ventilation louvers on the model so that they would appear to be hanging down - when in fact they were stretched horizontally," Taylor commented. "Some of them were fitted with hidden weights on a balance arm that could make them appear to swing slightly." The same model - rigged to fall on cue - was used for subsequent shots of the collapsing air shaft. "We took that miniature out to the parking lot and set it up on end so that we could easily create the effect of debris falling down as it collapsed." Grant McCune Design constructed all of the models used in the miniature shoot, conducted concurrently with the main unit photography in Rome. To circumvent communication problems in the long-distance working relationship, McCune and his chief designer, Smoky Stover, developed 'photo storyboards' for each of the miniature shots. After we went to Italy to check out the full-size setup," McCune recalled, "we started building a rough foamcore mockup of the sets. We photographed that mockup in black-and-white, then scanned the photographs into the computer, along with the original storyboards. Using Photoshop, we were able to manipulate pieces of the storyboards and apply them to the scanned-in photographs. We wound up with incredibly accurate 2-D representations of these shots, detailing what lens would be used, the lens angle, the film speed - everything. Once the storyboards were approved, McCune turned his efforts to the construction of models, including sixty-some cars that would stand in for the full-size vehicles in the more harrowing scenes inside the tunnel. Taking full advantage of a revolutionary plating technique, McCune quickly and efficiently produced dozens of near-perfect scaled replicas. In the course of four trips to Cinecitta, McCune photographed all of the vehicles used in the action sequences, then rented duplicate automobiles upon his return and had them scanned in three dimensions at TFX, a company that specializes in custom props and models. From those scans, TFX created quarter-scale clay maquettes. "We used the maquettes to make female molds, and from those we produced silicone males," McCune stated. "We sent them out to ArtCraft Plating & Finishing Company, where they were plated with nickel, in any thickness we wanted. So what we got back were fully metallic car models. All we had to do was slide the silicone molds out of the interiors, cut out the windows, slice open the doors and, in some cases, grind the thickness of the nickel down a bit to give us incredibly thin-walled, crunchable models. We painted them, stuck interiors into them and put them on chassis. Our place started to look like a miniature auto body shop." McCune's shop also reproduced sections of the tunnel in quarter scale - small sections employed for specific insert shots, and a seventy-foot-long version for more dynamic and involved action sequences. "We used the long miniature to photograph a flaming truck barreling toward camera," related Taylor, "and also for shots where you see cars swerving out of control, coming to a stop and then being blown back into the tunnel by the fire. Almost every shot of cars and fire together in the tunnel was filmed on the miniature setup." Although the special character fire featured throughout the explosion sequence would be generated by ILM, more generic displays were executed by pyrotechnician Richard Helmer in tandem with the models. "Richard was one of the unsung heroes of this affair," Taylor stated. "One of the problems we run into in shooting fire with miniatures is that CINEFEX 68 • 17 SHI 936

But Richard was able to produce a nice yellow-orange, smoky flame; and we managed to expose the film so that the look of that fire was retained." To propel burning and crashing vehicles through the tunnel miniature, the models were either towed by cable or radio controlled, depending upon the camera angle and nature of the specific shot. "For example," said Taylor, "in a scene in which a line of trucks explodes, it made sense to pull those models by cable since they were lined up and rigged with electrical connections to trigger explosions. We filmed that at 48 frames per second - which meant that the trucks had to move very quickly, starting way back in the tunnel in order to get up to speed. Then, in post, the little bit of exposed cable was removed digitally." Less linear shots, in which vehicles would be seen fishtailing and careening out of control, required the relative freedom of radio control. "The radio control models were piloted primarily by members of Grant's modelmaking crew - who also happen to be expert model racecar drivers. It took a great deal of skill to get the fancy moves we wanted out of radio control, especially since we were working within a tunnel that was only four feet wide " 18 • CINEFEX 68 The largest of the miniatures built for the show was an exterior tunnel entrance that duplicated the full-scale set at Cinecitta. "It was quarter scale, as well," stated Taylor, "but it still took up about a third of Grant's parking lot. We used that model to create shots of an overpass above the tunnel entrance collapsing, seen near the end of the explosion sequence, as well as scenes of the entrance itself collapsing onto cars trapped below." While the miniature unit was constructing and photographing the various models, ILM was attacking the problem of how to realize the explosion sequence fire that would roar through the tunnel, destroying everything in its path. As conceived by Rob Cohen, the fire effect was to be made up of three distinct images. "The first part is the leading edge," Cohen explained, "which is a rototiller of fire that chews up the oxygen as it moves through the tunnel. Following that is the fireball - a dense, red, gaseous wall of flame. Finally, there is what I called the plasma, an arm of fire that trails the fireball and extends all the way back to the origin of the explosion." Conceptualizing each of those distinct phases was one of the most problematic aspects of the Daylight assignment for ILM. "When I first met with "Scott Farrar stated, "we spent time Rob in Rome,' Sylvester Stallone flees a tumbling tank in a sequence orchestrated by hit West and ILM. talking about concepts for this - but being able to actually visualize it took a while. We had no visual reference, other than vague black-and-white storyboard drawings. Design-wise, it was a very difficult effect all the way through." In time, however, the concept gelled. "We began to see the leading edge as a rolling wave that would ride along the ceiling; and, after talking to Rob, we began to understand that the plasma aftermath would look something like what you see inside a kiln - a superhot, blownout yellowish color, with added qualities of movement and directionality. The fire would start out a typical orange as it impacted, then turn a superheated yellow in the plasma aftermath, with a lot of heat ripple distortion." Accounting for approximately half of the shots ILM would contribute to the show, the fire effects were achieved through a marriage of miniature and digital techniques, Real fire was filmed high-speed, by miniature unit director of photography Patrick Turner, on an all-black, quarter-scale tunnel, with the resulting imagery composited into plates shot on the full-size set at Cinecitta. "Inside the tunnel miniature," said Farrar, "were black shapes - we call them mandrels - that represented the full-size vehicles the fire would be moving over or wrapping around in the final composites. By manipulating our fire elements over and around these shapes, we could ensure that the flames would envelope the real cars correctly when they were composited into the backgrounds." The six-foot-wide, four-foot-tall tunnel miniature was built by the ILM model shop, under the supervision of Brian Gernand, and rigged with gas jets by Geoff Heron to create controllable bursts of flame. "With split-second timing, we could employ those jets to articulate and choreograph the roll and movement of the fire exactly," Farrar noted. "It was a little like marionetting fire. We adjusted the gas nozzles in tiny increments to get just the right look, refining the duration and aim of each spurt of fire. We didn't know if we could get a flame Rob would like using real, practical fire - but it was my preference to get it that way, if we could. It is difficult to produce a CG flame of any kind, let alone something as specific and unusual as this." Digital tools were used to enhance the practical effect, however. MICHAEL WESTMORE BEHIND THE MASKS article by Scott Essman Star Trek is more than Paramount Pictures' most successful franchise. It is also the dominant presence on the Paramount lot in the heart of Hollywood. Currently comprised of two weekly television shows and an eighth feature film just completed, the Star Trek empire inhabits nearly one-fourth of the studio's expansive soundstage and office space. In one of those busy, cluttered offices, Star Trek's supervising makeup artist, Michael Westmore, relaxes behind a desk reserved for fielding phone calls and watching video dailies. The Westmore name has been synonymous with film industry makeup since Michael's paternal grandfather, George, established the first motion picture makeup department in 1917 at Selig Studio, later to become MGM. In subsequent years, six Westmore sons made their mark in the industry: Mont, Michael's father, was Rudolph Valentino's makeup artist and supervised the makeup on Gone With the Wind; Frank worked for Cecil B. DeMille; Wally created Fredric March's makeup for Dr. Jekyll and Mr. Hyde; and Ern was a staple at RKO Pictures. But the two uncles who influenced young Michael the most were Perc - who created Charles Laughton's Hunchback of Notre Dame makeup - and Bud, who in 1945 succeeded the legendary Jack Pierce as head of Universal's makeup department. "I hung out at Bud's house on the weekends "Westmore recalled, while I was going to college,' "and in 1961, he offered me an apprenticeship at Universal. The first thing I worked on was Flower Drum Song." Westmore soon became the first apprentice for makeup great John Chambers, working on features such as The List of Adrian Messenger - where character makeups disguised the familiar faces of Tony Curtis, Frank Sinatra, Kirk Douglas, Burt Lancaster and Robert Mitchum - and in television, making up actors for the classic monster comedy, The Munsters, When Chambers went to Veteran makeup artist Michael Westmore has won an Academy Award and nine Emmys in his prolific thirty-five-year career. Twentieth Century Fox in 1968 to create the primate makeups for Planet of the Apes - for which he won a special Oscar - Westmore remained behind and was promoted to head of the makeup laboratory. After leaving Universal in 1970, Westmore spent the next five years researching therapeutic cosmetic aids for scarred accident victims and individuals with birth defects. From there he segued into his first stint as head makeup effects artist on a film - a little project nobody else wanted, entitled Rocky. Directed by John Avildsen, the movie was written by and starred an unknown Sylvester Stallone. A rags-to-riches tale set in the arena of professional boxing, Rocky would require makeups suggesting fighters' injuries. "I met Stallone over at MGM," Westmore recalled, "and he wanted to see something quickly. So I took a can of wax and created a swollen eye on him. He liked it, and that was the beginning. I made a cast of his face and started right away,." As the only makeup artist on the low-budget film, and with little time to prepare, Westmore enlisted Stallone's help in researching the fight sequences. "Sly got some old 8mm fight films and took them to his apartment on Sunset Boulevard. There was a punching bag hanging from the chandelier in the dining room, no furniture, and a big dog that ruled the house. In the bedroom, there was only a mattress on the floor. We sat on this mattress, with the door shut and the blinds drawn, watching these fight films and taking notes." With the films as reference, Westmore designed makeups for Stallone and Carl Weathers, who portrayed rival Apollo Creed. "When we were shooting the fights, I'd put Sly in one chair and Carl in the other. I'd make an eye piece for Carl, glue it on, color it, and then hand him the hair dryer so he could dry his eye while I was doing Stallone. I'd go back and forth between the two of them." Patterson was dispatched to East Africa, where the British government was attempting to complete the first railroad across the resource-rich continent. His mission - to build a bridge over the Isavo River - would have been difficult even if nothing had gone wrong. The location was remote and undeveloped, the river was mean and given to rise during the rains, and the construction schedule was too short by half. Then, into this nearly impossible situation came the Ghost and the Darkness, two rogue lions who, over the course of nine months, killed 133 members of Patterson's crew. Patterson recounted these astonishing events in his book, The Man-Eaters of Tsavo; and nearly a hundred years later, the story captured the attention of the film industry. Containing classic horror movie elements - cunning, relentless 'monsters'; victims isolated in a mysterious, exotic location; and a brave, resolute hero - The Man-Eaters of Tsavo was a natural. The involvement of director Stephen Hopkins, a longtime advocate of the project, and a screenplay by the venerated craftsman William Goldman only strengthened the story's cinematic potential; and the property was eagerly taken up by the production company founded by Michael Douglas and Steven Reuther. Although primarily a live-action movie pitting Patterson (Val Kilmer) and a hunter named Remington (Michael Douglas) against the two beasts, The Ghost and the Darkness could not have been realized without both visual and on-set effects. The former were assigned to visual effects supervisor Stuart Robertson and Sony Pictures Imageworks, while Stan Winston Studio provided the latter in the form of various animatronic lion rigs. THE CITY OF LOST CHILDREN MAGIC WITH A FRENCH TOUCH article by Alain Bielik Traditionally focused on character driven films, French cinema has been slow to follow in the footsteps of its most famous film pioneer - Georges Méliès - whose experiments a century ago with motion picture techniques are recognized as the basis of all modern-day cinematic effects. Spurred on by an interest in digital technology, however, French filmmakers have begun to pick up the pace - and nowhere is that more evident than in the work of directing duo Marc Caro and Jean-Pierre Jeunet. Having demonstrated a mastery of digital effects in commercials and in Delicatessen, their feature film debut, Caro and Jeunet recently captured the attention of film critics on both sides of the ocean with The City of Lost Children. A bizarre, adult fairy tale, filled with freak-show characters and startling imagery, the story revolves around a deranged, power-crazed scientist, Krank (Daniel Emilfork), aging prematurely because of an inability to dream. Aided by an odd assortment of disciples, Krank is behind the sinister disappearances of young children from the local port, abducted and taken to his lab on a mining rig at sea. There, the scientist attempts to steal their dreams, managing, however, only to live their nightmares. Oversight of the film's unique ambiance fell largely to Marc Caro. "I started as a graphic novel artist before going into traditional cel animation with Jean-Pierre," observed Caro, "so designing original environments has always been an integral part of our work. In this regard, we share the same background as Terry Gilliam or Tim Burton, with whom we've often been compared by the American media. The look of The City of Lost Children is the result of various influences - Jules Verne, Gustave Doré, graphic novel artist Tardi - all mixed up with our own sensibilities." Set in an unspecified time and place, the French fantasy The City of Lost Children - co-directed by Jean-Pierre Jeunet and Marc Caro - was filmed entirely on soundstages, but was opened up with digital matte paintings provided by Duboi. Updating the traditional fairy tale genre, Caro sought modern equivalents to such archetypal story elements as the castle. "We wanted the action to take place in a sea environment, because of the ambiance it offers," commented Caro. "From this starting point, we thought an old rig would nicely represent the traditional castle, with the classic evil sorcerer personified by our mad scientist. for the harbor city, we wanted a feeling of Venice and 19th-century London, while avoiding any reference to specific city or country. As in any fairy tale, the action takes place in an unspecified time and location." The red Victorian brickstones and the green Venetian waters would ultimately give the film its bi-color visual code. Shot entirely on soundstages near Paris, the film was lit in singular fashion by director of photography Darius Khondji. "We increased the colors on all the sets, props and costumes," explained Khondji. "Then, during the developing process at Motion Picture Film Development Lab, we did a bleach bypass on the interpositive - something which had never been done before - to tone them down to a normal level. The result was an image with shifted colors, which gave the film its distinctive look." The settings were brought to life by a cast of players selected for their physical ability to blend with the environment. Actors with strong or unusual facial features were specifically sought. "When you're dealing with such a shifted environment, you can't have 'normal' people in it," observed Caro. "That wouldn't work. All the elements had to blend seamlessly in order to create one believable, albeit unrealistic, universe, with each little detail contributing to that global shifted look. It was almost like painting." To handle the film's substantial effects load - encompassing 144 shots - Caro and Jeunet divided the work into different categories based on technique, assigning them to a number of specialized facilities. Also recruited was longtime partner Pitof, a digital effects supervisor at Duboi, Paris, who would supervise the effects plate photography and, with producer Antoine Simkine, oversee the digital effects. The movie opens with a young boy's vision of Christmas that quickly turns nightmarish as a dozen scary Santa Clauses invade his bedroom. THE ASSOCIATE GENDER BENDERS article by Estelle Shay In the 1994 comedy, Mrs. Doubtfire, makeup artist Greg Cannom won an Academy Award for his transformation of Robin Williams from middleaged doting dad into elderly female housekeeper. For his most recent assignment, The Associate, the goal was also a gender reversal - but of a rather different sort. Directed by Donald Petrie, the Hollywood Pictures comedy revolves around the efforts of struggling Wall Street financial analyst Laurel Ayres (Whoopi Goldberg) to penetrate the glass ceiling she encounters in the male-dominated world of high finance. Upon discovering that she has been cheated out of a well-deserved promotion by a duplicitous male colleague, she turns in desperation to an ingenious ruse - inventing a powerful white male associate to lend credibility to her work. Pressed to actually produce him when the ruse gets out of hand, Laurel eventually finds herself with no choice but to disguise herself as the fictitious financial whiz Robert S. Cutty. Recruited to the film about three months before shooting was scheduled to begin, Cannom approached the task of transforming the black actress into a Caucasian male with some trepidation. "My big concern was what to do with her hair. Whoopi has so much of it, my initial thought was: 'My God, this isn't going to work. We're going to have to design the makeup around the hair." To aid in the conceptual process, Cannom flew to South Carolina where the actress was on location for another project, and made a lifecast of her head down to her shoulders. Returning to his studio at Cannom Creations, he and artist Miles Teves did some drawings, then spent two weeks sculpting three full heads that incorporated several starkly different approaches to the character. "The director had suggested something like a 45-year-old jock type, or an older, Sydney Greenstreet kind of a As a Wall Street analyst who disguises herself as a fictitious male partner in The Associate, Whoopi Goldberg wore makeup by Greg Cannom. look," recalled Cannom. "So we did one sculpture that was very young, very athletic, with a strong jaw and chiseled features, and another that was a heavy, older man, about seventy. Since Whoopi had expressed a desire for the character to look like her good friend Marlon Brando - who had once observed that the two of them shared similar facial features - we also quickly bashed out a third sculpture that was a Brando type." When Goldberg and the producers favored the Marlon Brando look-alike, work was begun on a more refined sculpture, done in Roma clay on the head cast. "I resculpted the face, adding more weight and giving it a kind of today look, sixtyish in age," noted Cannom, "then Miles finished off the texturing and fine details. Actually, it was surprising how well it worked. To look at Whoopi, I never would have seen the resemblance, but in sculpting the head, I was amazed at how close her eyes and mouth were to Brando's. We stuck a wig on the finished sculpture and showed it to everyone, and they all loved it" In fashioning the makeup, Cannom elected to divide it into eight distinct pieces that could be applied separately. "When you do a head cast, things can droop a bit from the weight of the alginate, and throw it off," stated Cannom. "Because there was so much sculpture - especially over the eyes - I was really worried that if it didn't fit just right, I would end up having to resculpt the whole face. So I took a very thin dental spatula, and carefully divided the sculpture into sections. I cut the bottom lip out, then the line where the forehead separates from the sides of the face, then around the top lip and the nose, and so on." Mold shop supervisor Stephen Prouty made epoxy aluminum reinforced molds, and lab technician Roland Blancaflor ran the pieces in foam latex. The full set of appliances included a huge wraparound piece that covered the neck, chin and sides of the face, a forehead piece, a nose and upper lip section, two eyebags for the under-eye area, two lid and brow pieces to create saggy skin over the eyes, and a bottom lip piece. The 20th century was still a tew years away when a young writer named HI.G. Wells, fresh from completing his science fiction epic The Time Machine, moved from London to the English countryside to create new works of imagination. One of the stories born of his pastoral musings was The War of the Worlds, a terrifying tale of Martians invading earth, first serialized in Cosmopolitan in 1897. On the centennial eve of Wells' classic tale, bloodthirsty Martians return to earth in Mars Attacks!, a Christmas Warner Brothers release directed by Tim Burton and with a stellar ensemble cast. A filmmaker attracted to projects laced with macabre black humor and strange characters- as evidenced by previous offerings such as Beetlejuice and Edward Scissorhands - Burton was inevitably drawn to the delicious prospect of creating a film inhabited by rampaging Martians. But for the former Disney animator and funky effects fan who reenergized the art of stop-motion animation with The Nightmare Before Christmas, Mars Attacks! marked a turning point. After nearly two years of gearing up to produce stop-motion Martians and motion control spaceship models, Burton unexpectedly found himself presiding over an all-digital show. For his alien invaders - creepy creatures in green spacesuits and helmets that ballooned over big-brain heads and death-skull faces - Burton would engage Industrial Light & Magic to provide 300 shots featuring computer generated Martians. Some 140 spaceship and robot shots - also computer generated - would be assigned to Warner Digital Studios, a start-up effects house. The holiday season launch of Mars Attacks! arrived in the wake of the record-breaking boxoffice run enjoyed by Independence Day, a picture that paid homage to both classic flying saucer movies and the disaster films of the seventies. In contrast to the relatively straight-faced approach of that summer blockbuster, Mars Attacks! offered a cartoonish take on the alien invasion theme, derived from a 1962 trading card series infamous for its gory depictions of Martian-induced carnage. Co-created by the late Woody Gelman and Len Brown, the series had been released by Topps Chewing Gum, a company renowned for its baseball, television and movie tie-in trading cards. Those were the days of 'penny-a-pack' sets, when one cent got you a stick of gum and a card, while 'nickel packs' contained the extravagance of gum and six cards. But the Mars Attacks! cards were far different from the company's wholesome baseball and Davy Crockett offerings. Penciled layouts by comic book pro Bob Powell and final paintings by veteran pulp magazine illustrator Norm Saunders depicted horrific Martians with gigantic exposed brains and round white eyes set in skeletal faces. Moreover, each of the fifty-five cards featured grisly events with descriptive titles such as 'Destroying a Dog,' in which a horrified boy watches as a Martian death ray incinerates his beloved pet. Not surprisingly, the cards set off a howl of parental protest. There was some irony in the furor, however, given that only the previous year Gelman and Brown had been congratulated for a 72 1 CINEFEX 68

blood-and-guts trading card series marking the Civil War centennial-and much of that acclaim had come from those who would later defame their Martian invasion series. "Woody and I knew that educational stuff just didn't work on trading cards," recollected Len Brown, who today is a Topps creative director, "so we came up with the idea of doing the Civil War battles as graphically as we could get away with, with swords and bayonets and blood gushing. And we actually received letters from teachers thanking us for helping kids learn their history! The following year, Woody and I decided to do another gory, bloodand-guts series - the kids seemed to love it. We were both fans of science fiction movies, so we decided to do a space invasion series. We planned the pictures together, and I wrote the text on the backs of the cards. In many ways, we were trying to do everv science fiction movie cliché: we had big-headed aliens, Jant attacking bugs, ray guns and the like. It was War of the Worlds all over again." The Mars Attacks/ phenomenon might have remained in the sole province of card collectors - who today can pay as much as forty dollars for a single original issue card - if the Topps Company had not reissued the set in 1994 along with a companion comic book miniseries. The property caught the attention of Warner Brothers and was deemed a natural for Tim Burton, who had the same love for the sci-fi classics that had stirred the imaginations of Gelman and Brown. Burton's fondness for those movies extended to their old-fashioned photographic effects. Even the likes of Plan 9 from Outer Spacewith its paper plate flying saucer effects - was saluted by Burton in his Ed Wood. For Mars Attacks!, Tim Burton envisioned the employment of those same classic effects techniques, but with a modern twist -stop-motion Martians would be digitally composited into miniature spaceship interiors and live-action environments. Early in preproduction, a stop-motion team from England created the puppets, a miniature spaceship interior was built, and a promising test was produced. By September 1995, the production had signed Warner Bros. Imaging Technology - which had been formed the year before and had created a virtual fly-through of Gotham City for Batman Forever-to lay the groundwork for the anticipated fusion of hands-on animation and digital technology. But within the year, the stop-motion approach would be scrapped in favor of an all-CG approach and WBIT would be reorganized into Warner Digital Studios. "WBIT was originally set up for small-scale work,"explained WDS digital effects supervisor Guy Williams, "almost on a boutique level. But Warner Digital Studios was conceived to deal with as much Warner Brothers visual effects work as the studio wanted, while taking on outside work as well. So Warner Brothers brought in Mike Fink and Ellen Sommers to build a creative team and management structure that was capable of developing the facility into one that could deal with high-volume shows like Mars Attacks!" Helming Warner Digital's CG assignment for Mars Attacks! was visual effects supervisor Michael Fink, the creative head of the new company, whose resume included work with Douglas Trumbull on Star Trek: The Motion Picture and an Academy Award nomination for his first collaboration with Tim Burton on Batman Returns. At the start, Warner Digital's contribution to Burton's latest project was to be modest, since the Martians and spaceships were still slated to be achieved through stopmotion animation and miniature photography, respectively. However, among the stumbling blocks of the stop-motion approach were the helmets that supposedly enable the Martians to survive in the earth's atmosphere. To avoid the cleaning of the helmet glass that would be necessary prior to each frame of filming - a time-consuming task that would further burden the painstaking process of animating clusters of Martian characters throughout some 300 shots - the decision was made to construct the alien headgear digitally. "We produced a test in which we automatically tracked a CG helmet to tracking points around the rim of the Martian necks," Williams recalled. "The next thing we knew, the show had become all CG." With its only previous credits being some seventy shots for Eraserand work on the 3-D animated short Duck Dodgers, WDS was not awarded the entire show, even when the transition was made from stop-motion and miniatures to computer generated effects. "ILM had established quite a reputation for animating creatures," Mike Fink commented, "and at the time we were approached for Mars Attacks! our company was less than a year old. So it made sense for someone else to do the Martians and have us do the spaceships, which seemed the simpler of the two tasks. In the long run, I'm not so sure it was simpler. Our 140-shot count was a little deceiving because the total frame count exceeded most 200-shot shows." ILM's involvement in the project was equally indirect. Mars Attacks! producer Larry Franco had approached the company early on about digitally compositing the show's stop-motion elements- a development that sent up red flags for ILM visual effects producer Mark Miller. "We were nervous about going down that road," Miller admitted. "It was going to be a big 2-D compositing show, which meant that ILM was just going to be putting things together, with no way to control the animation or live-action elements. We thought that if the Martians were three-dimensional CG characters, we would have much more control in making them fit into the film environments. It would also allow Tim the freedom to change shots without having to reshoot. After we expressed our concerns, Larry told us to go ahead and out something together to show him " An ILM team that included Miller, visual effects supervisor Jim Mitchell, animation supervisor Dave Andrews and technical director Tim Mclaughlin produced a test showing three Topps-inspired, computer generated Martians composited into a live-action plate. The freedoms of the digital approach induced the studio to advance the projected spring 1997 delivery of Mars Attacks! to Thanksgiving 1996. That left ILM and Warner Digital with eight months in which to produce nearly 450 shots. Both companies began at full sprint, without the luxury of a preproduction planning period. For ILM, the goal was to produce cartoonishlooking aliens that would, nonetheless, integrate seamlessly into the live-action. That live-action ranged from early scenes of aliens addressing Congress - with the assembled legislators reduced to skeletons after some lethal death ray blasts - to the all-out interplanetary war that rages from Capitol Hill to Las Vegas and even Easter Island. "Tim wanted us to treat the Martians just like the other actors in the movie," Mitchell stated, "rather than treating them like effects." A similar conception phase was in the works at Warner Digital, where an early test was produced showing a hummingbirdlike CG saucer attacking the Egyptian pyramids. With input from Burton, the facility changed direction, ultimately conjuring up 180-foot-wide, ray blasting, multi-ton spaceships that mimicked the sci-fi saucers of old. "We had to create fiftiesstyle saucers and make them look as if they fit into the environment of a modern movie," explained CG lead Chris Wagner. "The saucers had to have this campy appearance; but unlike the fifties saucers, which flew in linear paths and could stop suddenly to blow something up, we tried to give our spaceships more of a personality, with oscillating movements." As production neared, troops at WDS and ILM were steeped in the Topps cards, drawing inspiration from their cartoonish rhythms and color schemes. For further inspiration, the Warner crew regularly popped in a videocassette of Earth us. the Flying Saucers, a 1956 Burton favorite that featured attacking stop-motion ships animated by Ray Harryhausen. Likewise, ILM art director Mark Moore - who for years had been assembling highlight reels loaded with classic and obscure film and television clips- opened Mars Attacks! dailies with crowd-pleasing selections from such fondly remembered 'B' flicks as Fiend Without a Face and The Angry Red Planet. Although both companies had to contend not only with performance issues but a looming production deadline, their work was facilitated by the keen animator's eye Tim Burton brought to the proceedings. "Tim is a director who has a good understanding of virtual effects and animation," marveled Williams. "You can show him things in an unfinished state and he'll look past the wire-frame or the flat shading and be able to see the motion and give you constructive criticism." "Some directors like to have total control," elaborated ILM's Chris Armstrong who, along with Linda Bel and Jenn Emberly, supervised specific Martian animation sequences, "almost as if they were doing the animation themselves. That can become extremely time consuming because everything goes through so many changes. Tim Burton seemed to trust us and be happy with what we were doing." While digital applications represented a creative departure for Burton, a Martian invasion movie was nothing short of radical for production designer Wynn Thomas. Thomas had been best known for designing Spike Lee's filmography, from School Daze and Do the Right Thing to Malcolm X and Jungle Fever. But the seeming incongruity of the Mars Attacks! assignment was precisely the point. "Designers can get typecast just like actors," Thomas noted. "It had come to the point where I was perceived only as an urban designer. So for the past couple of years I've tried to work on different types of projects. Even though this film had technical challenges, the design process is the same for each project- you do your research and find a way to connect to the material." Like the artists at ILM and WDS, Thomas turned to classic 'B' science fiction films and the Topps card series to breathe life into his design efforts. "The wonderful thing about the cards and those films is that they have their own quirky sense of fun shapes and colors," Thomas commented. "But the world isn't driven by primary colors- and film is a realistic medium. So, although the cards were the initial inspiration, the palette changed because we had to push the look away from the extreme color schemes of the cards, using those primary colors as accents only. And while Tim's intent was to create a movie that felt like a 1950s sci-fi picture, Mars Attacks! was covert in its spirit. Tim wanted a sense of timelessness, so we avoided things like cell phones or anything too obviously modern. Instead, we used cars from twenty years ago, generic props and neutral things that wouldn't lend themselves to placing the action in any particular year. We essentially did a period film without setting it in a specific period." Intruding on this timeless terrain were the cartoonish aliens and their otherworldly spacecraft. Although the CG units at ILM and Warner Digital followed the same basic animation process, the allocation of talent resources was fundamentally different - at least at first. At ILM, modelers routinely hand their work off to animators, who then turn their animation over to technical directors for the tackling of rendering and compositing issues. It is a process that, in many respects, recalls old-school animation techniques. "In traditional animation," noted Linda Bel, who arrived at ILM after five years at Disney, "there are animators who do the rough animation drawings, other artists who take those drawings and apply the final clean line, others who paint the backgrounds or do effects. There is a similar kind of breakdown in the CG department at ILM. We have people who specialize in building the models, others who create the actual animation, and still others who do the lighting and rendering. That means a lot of people are involved in each task, but it al-

lows people to play to their strengths." The initial notion at Warner Digital Studios was to give individual artists more control over their shots. "Our thought was to allocate each Mars Attacks/ shot to an individual artist," explained facility visual effects producer Lauren Ritchie. "That artist would not only do the animation, but also the lighting and even the final composite. We were, in some instances, able to do that - the approach seems to work especially well when all elements for a shot are CG-but with the number of shots that we had on this show, and the complexity of those shots, we ultimately fell back on a more traditional hierarchal system. I still feel the one-artist-does-all approach has merit because it gives the artist a feeling of ownership over a shot, as well as a full appreciation of what it takes to get a shot to final; but for this project, we found it best to break up the functions." We couldn't afford to pull any punches." For ILM, Mars Attacks! was an opportunity to shake any perceptions that the veteran company's look and style are solely photorealistic. "If people think ILM has a problem with doing funky effects, that's a misconception," Jim Mitchell stated. "We jumped at the chance to do this show. ILM can certainly do realistic stuff; but it's always fun to bring to life disproportioned, totally unrealistic characters. This was a wonderful opportunity to let our animators and technical directors run a little free. And I hope Tim Burton will come back and present us with another chance to bring his strange characters to life." Mars Attacks! also served as sweet vindication for card creator Len Brown, who has spent his life working in the ephemeral mediums of pulp magazines, comic books, genre films and trading cards - a medium that at one time was of appeal only to a small, cult-like tribe of connoisseurs, for whom co-creator Woody Gelman coined the code name Third Eyes. "Tim Burton is a Third Eye," Brown laughed, "and people who read Cinefex are very Third Eye. Back in the sixties, when Woody coined the term, it was unusual to find people who collected comics or were obsessed with genre films. Third Eyes were a subculture." Today, it is a Third Eye world. The top ten all-time grossing films are dominated by fantasy and science fiction themes, and glitzy conventions capitalize on the huge numbers of pop culture highrollers. Perhaps it all started a century ago, when the young H.G. Wells saw visions of Martian invaders laying waste to the countryside around him. The spectacles of fantasy that surround us today could indeed be the legacy of the inimitable writer, who was perhaps the seminal Third Eye diviner. BATTLE ACROSS THREE DIMENSIONS article by Estelle Shay

Since the advent of polarized glasses made it suitable for mass consumption, 3-D has held a special fascination for filmmakers. Seminal 3-D movies such as Bwana Devil and House of Wax achieved a modicum of success in the early fifties, but the novelty quickly wore off for all but the most die-hard of enthusiasts. A brief resurgence of interest in the eighties produced Jaws 3-D, and a few others; but for the most part, mainstream audiences- suffering eyestrain brought on by poor camera and projection techniques- remained disenchanted with the genre. When special venue demands led to a revival of 70mm widescreen film, the door was opened to a more suitable format for 3-D, and the technology took a significant leap forward with such attractions as Walt Disney World's Magic Journeys and, more recently, Honey, I Shrunk the Audience and Muppet Vision 3-D. Now, with the debut of Terminator 2: Battle Across Time at Universal Studios Florida, the envelope on 3-D cinematography has been expanded in a way no one thought possible. A continuation of the popular Terminator franchise that ignited the careers of writer-director James Cameron and superstar Arnold Schwarzenegger, the $60 million extravaganza deftly blends a theatrical stage show with an expansive 3-D film to provide a totally immersing experience that catapults viewers right into the middle of its nonstop thrills. The show, divided into three acts, begins in the present day, as audience members settle into an auditorium ostensibly belonging to Cyberdyne Systems. Midway through a demonstration of the company's latest advance in high-tech weaponry - the T-70 cyborg soldier - the show is interrupted, as renegades Sarah and John Connor rappel into the theater with guns blazing. Pursuing them from the future is the deadly T-1000, morphing into his familiar liquid metal form through a bullet hole blasted in the huge Cyberdyne logo mounted behind the stage. But before the T-1000 can dispatch his adversaries, another inhabitant of the future arrives in spectacular fashion, riding his trademark Harley-Davidson onto the stage through a time sphere that appears to open in the wall. With the T-1000 in hot pursuit, the Terminator grabs John and leaps back through the time portal, pulling the audience in with him as the presentation shifts from live stage show to 70mm 3-D film. Landing in the post-apocalyptic ruins of Los Angeles in the year 2029, the audience follows as the speeding motorcycle races through a war zone, fired upon by Hunter-Killer tanks and aircraft. On foot, the two take cover in a destroyed parking garage where they come under attack from a fleet of mini-HKs. Upon locating Skynet, the heart of the machine-ruled empire, they descend into its depths, intent on destroying its brain center. But first they must do battle with the ultimate killing machine - the deadly T-1,000,000. Four years in development, T2/3D was hardly what corporate executives at MCA/Universal had in mind when they first approached Gary Goddard, president of Landmark Entertainment Group, in the fall of 1992. Noted for its expertise in designing theme park attractions, Landmark had previously collaborated with MCA on a number of crowd-pleasers, including Kongfrontation, Conan, Ghostbusters and Jaws. Their newest assignment, however, had Goddard and senior show designer Adam Bezark stymied. "They wanted us to come up with a concept for a stunt show based on Terminator 2: Judgment Day, "recalled Goddard. "We watched the picture over and over, looking for a hint as to how we might do it. T2 is a compelling story, but the action segments are essentially three fantastic Jim Cameron chases, plus some spectacular morphing." Reluctant to return empty-handed, Goddard and Bezark wrestled with the assignment for a week. "To break the logjam, we asked ourselves, "If we were going to do a morph on stage better than in the film, how would we do it? And very quickly, 3-D came to mind. Then we thought: What if it's a 3-D morph on multiple screens that suddenly surround you? And what if we combine it with live actors that appear to jump in and out of the screen?' From there, the ideas just started cascading." Having fleshed out their concept on paper, Goddard contacted MCA to arrange a meeting. "We told them up front: What we're about to present to you is not a stunt show. It's something ten times better - something that's never been done before." Sufficiently intrigued by the pitch, studio executives gave a nod for Landmark to develop a more detailed presentation. In addition to a buyoff from MCA, the project would also require approvals from Terminator 2 principals Mario Kassar of Carolco Pictures, producer Gale Anne Hurd and, of course, James Cameron. "Whatever we came up with, we knew that not only would it have to serve MCA's purposes, it would also have to be something Jim Cameron could get excited about. We'd have to really push the envelope." In December 1992, armed with MCA's endorsement, a thirtypage treatment, detailed storyboards, more than a hundred color sketches and preliminary designs, Goddard and Bezark met with Cameron. "We were thinking: 'Oh God, we're pitching this to the guy who created the Terminator films - it's his characters, his creation. How is that going to go over?' But we knew that Jim liked new technologies; and a big part of what we were promoting was the idea that we would be pushing the boundaries of 3-D. We were counting on the fact that he might be intrigued by the opportunity to explore a new medium. That turned out to be a good call." Somewhat skeptical going in, Cameron quickly warmed to the presentation, even going so far as to suggest that he might be interested in taking on a more active role in the project. "My initial contribution," recalled Cameron, "was to sell Universal on the idea that we get the actual cast and do it like a real movie, as opposed to their idea of using generic actors. They thought the Terminator could have his face mostly blown off, and you wouldn't really see that it wasn't Arnold. But I couldn't see how that would work. "We knew from the start that it would be computer generated," stated Darren Gilford, who designed the creature. "In the beginning, we wanted something so scary and evil-looking that I was kind of getting away from traditional icons like head, legs and arms. So I had to pull back a little and create more recognizable features The final nightmarish vision was that of a polyalloy arachnid-like monster, with jaws, fangs and pupil-less eyes, six razor-sharp legs and two long, tentacled arms. "What made it so challenging," remarked Spiteri, who supervised the task, "was that the T-Meg goes through a life cycle. It starts out as part of the environment. Since it needed to have maximum flexibility to meet the complex animation demands, he developed a technique that allowed him to create the geometry as one continuous surface. "If I had created the legs or arms as separate objects," Robichaud explained, "they probably would have shown seams in the animation, and not allowed us much as far as morphing capabilities. "We felt a great deal of pressure on this sequence," Dutton remarked. "We knew it was absolutely critical to Rob that the final moments of the film seem completely real - yet everything conspired against us. The best we could do was shoot doubles in warmer water somewhere else and pray for similar light. The actor closeups captured at Cinecitta were photographed by Bill Taylor in a bluescreen tank. "The idea for the bluescreen setup was something I borrowed from Art Cruikshank, who was one of the great visual effects guys at Disney," said Taylor. "At one point, Art had come up with the idea of placing a small tank in front of a bluescreen - or, back then, a sodium screen - and putting the actor CINEFEX 68 • 135

in the tank, which would create a reflection of both the actor and the bluescreen in the water. Usually, you do everything you can to prevent the bluescreen from reflecting. But in this case, we wanted it to reflect, because that reflected blue allowed us to lift the actor, his reflection, plus any wave or ripples in the water surrounding him, and matte all of that into another plate. I had been wanting to try out Art's idea for years - and this was the ideal opportunity." A pump system that continuously drained and refilled the tank provided a constant flow of water. Benjamin Fernandez built a weir that directed the water overflow toward the bluescreen side of the tank, where it poured over the edge in a smooth stream. "Doing that created an imperceptible join between the bluescreen and its reflection," Taylor explained, "and the weir itself didn't show because water was flowing over it. With that setup - and some roto touch-up in post - the actors existed in a kind of blue limbo, with blue surrounding them in all directions. We did about four different setups with the bluescreen water tank, in addition to a couple of downshots that we processed to take the blue reflections out of the water and replace them with gray sky. It worked beautifully." The bluescreen tank photography of Brenneman and Stallone was composited into a low-angle Hudson River plate that had been photographed from the Colgate Pier in Manhattan. The camera, which was mounted to a crane, began tight on the two characters, then pulled back into a wider aerial shot revealing rescue units arriving at the scene. "The camera holds on Madelyne and Kit as they swim toward a Coast Guard boat," related Taylor, "then tips up to reveal Manhattan off in the background. One of the biggest challenges in compositing the sequence was that the lighting in the river backgrounds was very bright and sunny; but they were being cut in back-to-back with the aerial shot of Manhattan, which had been photographed when it was foggy and overcast. We spent weeks creating paint elements and doing color and local contrast adjustments to make those brightly lit, perfectly clear backgrounds look overcast." As the pullback extends into the wider aerial view, the bluescreened images of the actors are replaced by stunt doubles filmed at Lake Castaic in Southern California. To achieve a composite that would place the doubles into the river background, aerial pullbacks - photographed by a SpaceCam mounted to a helicopter - were executed at both the New York and Lake Castaic locations. 136 • CINEFEX 68 A multi-gyroscope system, SpaceCam digitally records camera pan, tilt and zoom, while maintaining a stable image even from unstable platforms such as helicopters or airplanes. Although the system has been in use within the film industry for several years, Daylight was the first production to utilize its most recent innovation - new technology that employs a satellite hookup to determine and record, in real time, the helicopter's precise position in terms of longitude, latitude and height to within an accuracy of mere inches. In the case of the Hudson River pullback, that information enabled the filmmakers to produce two matchingperspective aerial plates - one in New York and the other at Lake Castaic - with the helicopter recreating its relative position at the first site when shooting at the second. With two aerial pullbacks having exactly matching perspectives and angles, assembling of the composite was fairly simple. The technology behind such accurate positioning data was developed jointly by SpaceCam Systems and Trimble Navigation. "It works in conjunction with the Global Positioning System," said SpaceCam president Ron Goodman, "which is a constellation of satellites developed by the military for navigational purposes. Each of those satellites is linked together, so they emit synchronous signals, from which the exact position of any receiver can be determined. It is a precise, automated system that allows you to calculate your position at any time - on the face of the earth or above the face of the earth - with an accuracy of under two feet, But what was developed by Trimble Navigation - called differential GPS - exceeds the military resolution, and can determine the position of a receiving antenna within one centimeter of latitude, longitude and altitude. What we did was integrate Trimble's technology with the SpaceCam system. So while SpaceCam solves the problems of stability and control in aerial photography, this innovation solves the problem of determining exact position when filming from a platform in space." A decidedly more low-tech aid that guided the Illusion Arts team in compositing the pullback was a giant target - comprised of white balls arrayed in a triangle - that was positioned in the Hudson to mark the area to be occupied by Madelyne and Kit. A similar target was placed in the water at Lake Castaic. "That target made it fairly easy for Richard Patterson and David Williams in our computer department to match-move the Lake Castaic film to the Hudson River film," noted Taylor, "with some very artful articulate rotomattes around the swimming characters. Unfortunately, it was a nice bluesky, sunshiny day at Lake Castaic when we shot the helicopter film, so we had to suppress the blue color in that plate to get it to match the overcast Hudson River background." In addition to its composite shots, Illusion Arts contributed matte paintings to extend both night and daytime exterior wide views of the Manhattanside tunnel entrance - which had been built in full-scale at Cinecitta, but only to a height of two stories. Syd Dutton, who was integrally involved in the conception and execution of the matte paintings, also supervised the photography of the fullscale set in Rome. "For these wide shots," Dutton related, "our vantage point was very high - so we had to reveal additional levels of the tunnel, the roof, surrounding buildings and the Hudson River in the middle distance. In both daytime and nighttime shots, everything but the two-story tunnel entrance set is a matte painting." The digital paintings featured 3-D animated elements - created by Fumi Mashimo - such as boats, helicopters and searchlights, as well as traditional touches such as moving clouds and smoke from chimneys. The river was simulated with a combination of real water elements and computer animation. Seen later in the film, the night painting also featured the collapsed tunnel, along with police cars, helicopters and rescue vehicles. Both paintings were executed by Robert Stromberg and Mike Wassel. "We have always used animated elements to add life to our matte paintings," Dutton commented, "but the computer has greatly increased the range and flexibility of those elements. The ability to fly a helicopter through a scene in any path we choose, or to have complete control over interactive lighting effects, has introduced a whole new level of creative possibilities." Opening on December 6, Daylight was the second Rob Cohen film to be released within a sixmonth period. The grueling three years that had produced both the new movie and Dragonheart had finally come to a close, leaving the weary director to ruminate on what he had accomplished. "These two films threw me into the deep end of the pool, effects-wise," Cohen observed. "On the first, there was an all-CG leading character to deal with; and on this one, there was the blowout - without a doubt, the most difficult effects sequence I've ever been up against. So, even though they overlapped in a really brutal way, Dragonheart and Daylight were tremendous learning experiences, and I don't regret taking them both on in the way I did."

With the live-action footage obtained, Mack turned his attention to the mice men themselves. A twelve-inch maquette fashioned by Stan Winston Studio was digitized to create a basic 3-D computer model. To animate that model, Mack donned a motion capture suit and performed the mice men actions. "Once we had this motion capture data, we were able to cut and splice pieces of it together with tools written by Dennis Blakey in Prisms 3-D software," Mack explained. "The next step was to apply those actions and movements to the mice men - just as we'd done with the tiger actions and the Lo-Mai skeleton. We used the tools written by Dennis to do a best fit of the motion capture onto the mouse man computer skeleton. If the motion was not quite right, we modified it. We also did a lot of secondary animation to correct bits of action and movement, and to add the tails. For the facial animation, we did facial capture, with Dennis providing the facei Secondary deformations were also applied to create breathing movements, muscle bulging and a bit of shake in the abdomen as the creatures jumped and landed on hard surfaces. "To make the tracking easier," stated Mack, "we had surveyed the whole set with laser equipment, measured everything carefully and taken lots of photographs. From there it was just a matter of lighting, rendering and applying fur to each creature." The creation of fur had been one of the key concerns, for both the mice men and the Lo-Mai characters. "Simon O'Connor wrote a fur shader for us from scratch," Mack said. "We took a volumetric approach to it, which meant that instead of there being actual geometry for each hair, the fur was created basically as a rendering trick, with an algorithmic function determining where a hair would be and where it would not be. The result was that we could have as much hair as we wanted and the render time would not be any slower. So we didn't have to count hairs. Since we had twenty-some mice men - nine of which would be on screen at the same time - as well as Lo-Mai, we didn't want to worry about the amount of fur we could render at any one time. With this shader, we could control the length of fur, its density, its color and its distribution with texture maps. It was great to be able to control all of that explicitly, rather than have it an inherent part of the fur shader. I painted all the maps for sores and specularity, the color and bumpiness of the skin, as well as the maps that drove the fur." Plagued by nightmare logistics, horrendously short deadlines, rugged locations, torrential rains, forty-knot winds, cast changes and disturbingly sudden shifts in both direction and director, The Island of Dr. Moreau seemed to support one popular filmmaker's contention that making a movie is war. But despite the many difficulties, the warriors at Digital Domain and Stan Winston Studio came away from the experience with the gratifying conviction that their own battles, at least, had been won. "It was an extremely difficult shoot," Stan Winston concluded, "conducted under the most adverse of conditions. But all of the artists were as dedicated as they were talented, and they worked their tushes off on this show. Because of that, they pulled it off beautifully. I was very proud."
